articles.title: Trump says FBI probing Nvidia CEO Huang as China controversy deepens
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday the FBI was looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman...
articles.body:
By Steve Holland, Courtney Rozen, Karen Freifeld and David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday the FBI was looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Trump said he "was amazed" by allegations about Huang, ‌among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that ‌the woman was a spy.

"I know the FBI is looking into it," Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape," he added.

Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% on Monday after the company's board launched ​an internal investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

The probe, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on 63-year-old Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.

The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.

He ‌is Nvidia's fifth-largest shareholder with a roughly 3.6% stake, according ⁠to LSEG data, and keeps a tight grip on the company through an unusually flat structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him.

But unlike Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms or Elon Musk's SpaceX, Nvidia has no dual-class shares that would give co-founder Huang majority ⁠voting control.

The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed on Huang's relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that the president chose not to act on the information.

"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.

Huang's relationship with Trump ​has ​coincided with several favorable policy developments for the company, and the president has lavished Huang with praise, ​awarding him the nation's highest honor for scientific achievement in October.

The ‌same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million of Nvidia shares during the summer.

Nvidia said its board has confidence in Huang, thought by many on Wall Street to be the most important person underpinning the AI trade. Analysts acknowledged uncertainty around succession, but most do not expect the investigation to result in the longtime CEO stepping down.

articles.title: The stock market is doing some of the Fed's dirty work
articles.summary: A new analysis from DataTrek co-founder Nicholas Colas suggests the recent volatility on Wall Street may be enough to do some heavy lifting for the Fed.
articles.body:
The odds of a Fed rate hike are creeping upward . A strong jobs report last week cemented the argument further for another raise. And inflation figures coming later today are expected to confirm that pricing pressures remain stubbornly high.

Together, that's a compelling case — elevated pricing pressures call for a hike, while healthy jobs figures provide cover for tamping down the economy.

The odds for a 25 basis point hike at the Fed's December meeting are over 80%, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

But a new analysis from DataTrek co-founder Nicholas Colas suggests that the recent volatility on Wall Street is also doing some heavy lifting for the Fed — potentially removing the need for subsequent hikes next year.

"Stock market volatility and lower equity prices are one definition of 'tighter financial conditions,'" Colas wrote in the note. That means that Fed funds futures see the recent action on Wall Street as reducing the need for the central bank to intervene.

After the expected hike next month, the market forecasts the Fed will stay the course through at least the first quarter of 2027. Chances of the next increase aren't considered likely until April. Overall odds of a more hawkish rate policy have diminished, with the odds for no or one hike in 2027 now at 68%, up from 57% a week prior, Colas said.

One of Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's catchphrases is that "markets are doing some of the Fed's work for it." As Colas noted, that's increasingly coming true.

But recent tech jitters can also make the Fed's job more difficult, adding another layer of uncertainty and reorienting the public's expectations on top of the fact that the market and the Fed respond to each other .

If the tech sell-off takes off again and markets begin to anticipate a troubled growth story, the Fed might jump to action to reassure Wall Street. Right now, a little bit of selling is saving the Fed from some trouble. But a heavier dose of pessimism could be self-reinforcing.

articles.title: Man sold two properties for Rs 47.54 lakh and received cash payments for them; he paid capital gains tax, yet faced penalty, but ITAT Cuttack cancels it because tax officer invoked wrong section
articles.summary: What if you sell properties but receive the payment in cash?
articles.body: What if you sell properties but receive the payment in cash? Despite recording capital gains in your tax return, are you still likely to face penalties from the Income Tax Department?The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Cuttack, has ruled in favour of a taxpayer who was penalised for accepting cash from the sale of properties, despite having declared the transactions in his income tax return and paid the applicable capital gains tax.What the case is about:The case concerned a man in Odisha who, according to the submissions before the tribunal, sold two properties for a combined consideration of around Rs 47.54 lakh. However, for this sale he received the entire amount in cash. The person in question disclosed the property transactions in his income tax return (ITR) and paid the capital gains tax due on the sales.The Income Tax Department's Centralised Processing Centre (CPC) in Bengaluru processed his return and accepted his computation of capital gains tax.However, the Assessing Officer (AO) in Berhampur, Odisha, subsequently received information indicating that the man had collected the Rs 47.54 lakh sale proceeds in cash. The AO initiated an investigation, which established that the taxpayer had accepted cash payments for the property transactions.The AO then invoked Section 269SS, read with Sections 271D and 273D, and held that receiving the sale consideration in cash amounted to a violation of Section 269SS, according to an ET report. A penalty was consequently imposed on the man who challenged it before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), or CIT(A).However, the appeal was rejected. He then approached the ITAT in Cuttack, where he secured a favourable ruling on October 5, 2026.Why did the taxpayer win the case?The man’s counsel argued that the assessing officer had invoked the wrong section of the Income-tax Act to impose a penalty for accepting cash against the sale of property. He also cited a decision by a coordinate bench of ITAT Cuttack in the case of Satyabrata Panda, dated March 16, 2026, in which the penalty had been cancelled under similar circumstances.After examining the facts, ITAT Cuttack held that Section 269SS did not apply to the transactions for which the AO had sought to impose a penalty under Section 271D. The tribunal also referred to the decision in Satyabrata Panda and noted that a similar issue had arisen in the case of Arati Saraf, where the AO had relied on an incorrect provision of the Income-tax Act to levy a penalty.The tribunal concluded that the AO should have invoked Section 269ST rather than Section 269SS. Since the penalty had been imposed under Section 271D on the basis of the latter provision, ITAT Cuttack cancelled it.However, the cancellation of the Section 271D penalty does not mean that the tribunal declared the cash receipt exempt from all other provisions of the Income-tax Act.Pranshu G, Partner at Ashok Pranshu & Co, told ET that the taxpayer succeeded because the ITAT, Cuttack, considered the cash to be the sale consideration received upon completion of the property transaction, rather than an advance covered by Section 269SS.On this basis, the tribunal set aside the penalty imposed under Section 271D. It held that Section 269ST and the corresponding penalty provision, Section 271DA, were the relevant provisions in the circumstances of the case.Pranshu explained that the matter concerned penalty proceedings and did not involve prosecution. He also pointed out that the Income Tax Department could potentially initiate fresh proceedings against the man under the applicable provision. However, any such move would have to take into account the limitation period prescribed under Section 275.According to Pranshu, courts have differed on whether the requisite satisfaction must be recorded during assessment proceedings before a penalty can be initiated. He added that the Income Tax Department cannot use a change in the applicable statutory provision to revive proceedings for which the limitation period has already expired.Pranshu advises property sellers who have received payments in cash to disclose the entire sale consideration without delay, calculate their capital gains accurately and pay the applicable tax along with interest. They should also check whether they remain eligible to file a revised or updated income tax return for the relevant year.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.standfirst: El precio de la luz se abarata este martes
articles.summary: El precio de la luz se abarata este martes
articles.body: El precio medio de la electricidad en el día de hoy es de 171,39 €/MWh, lo que representa una disminución de 8,28 € en comparación con el día anterior, que cerró en 179,67 €/MWh. Este ajuste se produce en un martes, cuando muchos consumidores comienzan la semana laboral. A medida que avanza la jornada, se analizarán las horas más caras y más baratas para gestionar mejor el consumo energético. Los precios de la electricidad alcanzan sus niveles más altos entre las 18:00 y las 21:00 horas, consolidándose como el periodo más costoso del día. Durante esta franja horaria, se observan valores que superan los 200 €/MWh, con picos que llegan a los 219.8 €/MWh y 220.63 €/MWh. Este bloque continuo de horas caras resalta la tendencia de los precios a crecer en la tarde y primera parte de la noche. La electricidad es más barata en las primeras horas de la madrugada y al mediodía, con oportunidades significativas de ahorro. Las franjas horarias más relevantes para reducir el costo son entre las 11:00 - 12:00 (108.72 €/MWh), 12:00 - 13:00 (90.18 €/MWh) y 13:00 - 14:00 (90.98 €/MWh), donde se registran los precios más bajos, especialmente destacando una ventana efectiva de precios bajos entre las 11:00 y las 14:00. Además, en la madrugada, el tramo más económico es de 03:00 - 04:00 (155.63 €/MWh) a 04:00 - 05:00 (142.4 €/MWh). De esta manera, se pueden identificar momentos óptimos para un ahorro considerable. En el análisis de los precios de la electricidad para el día de hoy, destaca una clara concentración de las horas más caras en la franja de la tarde, que se extiende desde las 17:00 hasta las 21:00, donde los precios superan los 200 €/MWh. Este patrón resulta relevante para el consumidor, ya que indica los momentos del día en los que se debe tener especial atención para evitar gastos innecesarios.

articles.title: Gas prices fall below $4 per gallon for the first time since July
articles.summary: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from motor club AAA.
articles.body: The average nationwide price for regular gasoline Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from motor club AAA. The drop comes as oil prices have plunged, with President Donald Trump repeatedly playing down the prospect of renewed strikes on Iran, and pushing for progress between Russia and Ukraine in new trilateral talks. Still, gas prices remain elevated by more than 30% since Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched the Iran war Feb. 28, and around 40% since the beginning of the year. The drop in pump prices came after oil futures plunged 13% last week. For the global crude oil benchmark Brent, it was its biggest one-week percentage drop since April 2020, when the Covid pandemic began shutting down the global economy and demand for oil rapidly declined. Oil prices slid by another 5% Monday, to their lowest point since Aug. 31. And Tuesday, they briefly fell below $90 a barrel. The slide in oil prices started after Trump told NBC News last week that he did not plan to attack Iran. The fall continued after Democratic candidates put up commanding vote totals in Tuesday’s midterm elections, which some called a “blue tsunami.” Markets quickly began betting that Democratic control of the House and the Senate would put a cap on some of Trump’s most economically disruptive policies, such as the Iran war. “Given the Democrats’ control of Congress, there will likely be more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult,” ING commodities strategists said in a note. “The outcome of the elections means there could be more pushback from the Republican Party, too.” “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a post on social media in the wake of the results Wednesday morning. Vance added that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” For traders, Vance’s acknowledgment of the unpopularity of the war bolstered the case for lower oil prices. But Friday, Trump was briefed on a narrow window for a potential new military campaign against Iran, sources told NBC News. No decision has been taken, the officials also said. Trump on Monday again reinforced that he was leaning against a major escalation. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” the president told reporters at the White House. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” He said there was there was “positive momentum” in talks and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.” He added that “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.” As a result of the newly-set market expectations and the decline in oil prices, consumer relief at the pump was swift, with more likely in coming days. The nationwide average regular gas price, which was $4.14 on Election Day, has already fallen to $3.97. Diesel prices have also fallen sharply in recent days, from $6.28 per gallon on Election Day, to $6.15, which could take even more pressure off consumers at the grocery store or during their holiday shopping trips. The rise in diesel prices, economists say, can quickly spill over into inflation on grocery and department store shelves, given that the fuel is critical for transporting goods around the country and world on trains, ships and trucks. The rise in diesel has been far more than the rise in gas prices, with the commercial fuel still elevated by more than 70% since the start of the year, due to not only the Iran war, but also continued attacks on energy infrastructure in the Ukraine-Russia war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has promised to continue striking Russian energy assets, in retaliation for attacks on his country. Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has historically been one of the largest diesel exporters to the rest of the world. The U.S. is hosting talks between Russia and Ukraine n Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first trilateral negotiations since February. But analysts warn that oil markets still face several significant risks, which could limit further downside, or spark another price surge. “How all this plays out is still highly uncertain,” ING’s team said, adding that in its assessment “the degree and speed to which the oil market has sold off seems to be overdone.” Oil markets will also need to support the refilling of hundreds of millions of barrels of reserves that have been emptied this year in an attempt to keep a lid on prices. The U.S. strategic petroleum reserve currently contains the smallest amount of crude oil since 1982. Citigroup commodities analysts noted that “the period between now and January 3rd, when the new Democratic Congress is seated, is a ‘lame duck’ window during which the White House could seek to advance foreign policy objectives as well as personnel changes with fewer political constraints.” “This period could see either accelerated dealmaking or renewed escalation, meaning markets could remain choppy even if the longer-term direction points to eventual diplomatic resolution,” they wrote. Already, Trump has announced some changes. On Friday, Susie Wiles left the White House as Trump’s chief of staff, replaced by Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration crackdown. Citi’s team also said that the recent Israeli elections could have implications for oil prices. “The recent inconclusive Israeli elections mean that Prime Minister Netanyahu could continue to pressure the US to be more hawkish on Iran for the moment.” On Saturday, Netanyahu’s long tenure came a step closer to ending. Israeli President Isaac Herzog handed Netanyahu’s rival Gadi Eisenkot the chance to form the country’s next government. But, for at least the next six weeks, Netanyahu remains in place.

articles.title: Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China
articles.summary: US lawmakers call for tighter restrictions on chip sales amid inquiry into Nvidia CEO’s relationship with alleged spy.
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s intimate relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy has highlighted divisions in Washington over the export of advanced chips to China.

Huang, the head of one of the most critical firms in the global artificial intelligence race, has long been among Silicon Valley’s most powerful voices arguing against restrictions on high-end chip sales.

For years, the tech executive lobbied United States President Donald Trump to loosen export controls, finding allies in sympathetic administration figures such as David Sacks, Trump’s former AI tsar.

Whereas hawkish voices argued that Beijing should not have access to cutting-edge US technology on national security grounds, Huang and like-minded executives argued that China already had the computing power to make strides in AI and that wider uptake of US technology would help maintain its dominance in the field.

Jensen Huang’s lobbying now faces intense scrutiny following claims that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — with whom he had an affair — was an intelligence agent recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims, which The New York Times and the Financial Times first reported, citing unnamed US intelligence officials.

Nvidia’s board of directors on Sunday launched an inquiry into Jensen Huang’s relationship, pledging to examine “all available information” while also expressing confidence in the CEO.

Jensen Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, has pledged to cooperate fully with the inquiry and expressed his commitment to protecting Nvidia and US national security.

Trump has meanwhile said the FBI too is investigating whether Huang’s affair led to any compromise on US national security.

Already, US lawmakers have invoked the controversy to push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to US chips.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks on Monday called on the US Congress to take “decisive action” and pass their AI Overwatch Act, which would empower lawmakers to scrutinise and potentially halt exports of advanced chips to China and other adversaries.

“The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes and ensure that advanced AI chips are not going to China’s military,” Warren and Banks said in a joint statement.

Democratic House Representative Bill Foster also cited Jensen Huang’s relationship in a statement on Monday in which he called on his fellow lawmakers to get his Chip Security Act “across the finish line”.

The legislation, cosponsored by Republican House Representative Bill Huizenga, aims to prevent illicit smuggling to countries such as China by implementing measures to track the location of chips sent overseas.

Advocates of tighter restrictions now have a “much stronger political argument” and are likely to make use of it, said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and founder of Tech Buzz China.

“Chip exports to China have been deeply divisive in Washington, and Huang has been one of the strongest advocates for keeping that market open,” Ma told Al Jazeera.

“If his influence is diminished by this investigation, regardless of its eventual findings, those pushing for tighter restrictions will be in a much stronger position,” she said.

Trump, who has forged a close relationship with Jensen Huang since returning to the White House, has taken several actions to make it easier for chip makers to do business with China, while also maintaining significant export controls.

In May last year, the US Department of Commerce announced that it would scrap the previous Biden administration’s “AI Diffusion Rule”, which would have imposed caps on chip exports to more than 100 countries, including some US allies.

In December, Trump said he had granted Nvidia approval to sell its second-most powerful chip, the H200, to China under an arrangement that would see 25 percent of sales paid to the US government.

Nvidia, which controls an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the market for graphics processing units (GPUs) used to run frontier AI, welcomed the decision at the time, saying it would “support high-paying jobs and manufacturing in America”.

On the other hand, Trump has resisted calls to allow exports of Nvidia’s top-of-the-line Blackwell chips, which deliver about 2.5 times the performance of the H200.

“I think recent events likely increase attention on export control loopholes, and add momentum to bills already being discussed in Congress, like the Chip Security Act,” Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, a Washington, DC-based think tank, told Al Jazeera.

While export controls have spurred contentious debate, their effectiveness has been called into question amid China’s steady advances in AI development.

Authorities and analysts have documented widespread smuggling of restricted chips into China, mainly through Southeast Asia.

Chips with compute power equivalent to 1.6 million Nvidia H100s made their way to China in violation of export restrictions up to the end of 2025, according to an estimate by Epoch AI.

Chinese companies have also been able to bypass US law by remotely accessing compute capacity supplied by Nvidia-powered data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

Gabriel Wildau, managing director at global business advisory firm Teneo, said claims that Huang had been ensnared in an espionage campaign deserved to be treated with skepticism given the anonymous leaks and motives to discredit him and his company.

“President Trump shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement, but he may face new pressure from Congress and hawkish voices inside his administration to address the remote access issue,” Wildau, who focuses on political risk analysis in China, told Al Jazeera.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have already met twice this year: The US president visited Beijing in May, and the Chinese leader reciprocated with a state visit to Washington in September. They are scheduled to meet again next week when Trump visits Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. And they are expected to meet a fourth time in 2026 in December, when Trump hosts the G20 summit in Miami.

“The risk is that Washington acts to close this loophole [in the aftermath of the Huang controversy], and Beijing regards the action as a violation of the bilateral truce,” Wildau said, referring to the trade truce Trump struck with Xi during their summit in South Korea last year.

Chris Clague, an associate fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said the revelations about Jensen Huang would inevitably undermine the “legitimate” argument in favour of allowing tech transfers between the US and China.

“This has made it a little bit easier for his detractors to poke holes in that,” Clague told Al Jazeera. “It’s indicative of the tensions that exist between the US and China, which are never going away, but it shouldn’t derail efforts at finding some sort of compromise.”

articles.title: Honda raises full-year profit outlook, books $3 billion in EV-linked costs in Q2
articles.summary: TOKYO, Nov 10 () - Honda raised its annual profit forecast by 20% on Tuesday, as it ‌expected robust demand for hybrid vehicles and a ‌boost from a weaker ye...
articles.body:
TOKYO, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Honda ( HMC ) raised its annual profit forecast by 20% on Tuesday, as it ‌expected robust demand for hybrid vehicles and a ‌boost from a weaker yen to help offset slumping sales in ​China.

Honda stock fell more than 1% before the bell on Tuesday.

Japan's second-largest automaker raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen ($4.94 billion) from 650 billion yen.

The company booked 484.8 billion yen in costs linked to the ‌restructuring of its ⁠electric-vehicle business in the second quarter, causing it to report a surprise drop in profit ⁠for the period.

Operating profit for the July-to-September quarter fell 39% from a year earlier to 118 billion yen, ​well below ​the 250 billion yen ​median forecast in a ‌poll of nine analysts by LSEG.

It booked more than $9 billion in EV-restructuring-related charges in the previous financial year, pushing the firm into its first annual loss in nearly 70 years in May.

Honda is betting heavily on hybrid ‌vehicles, particularly in the US, ​its top market. US sales ​rose 9% in the ​second quarter and accounted for half of ‌its global retail sales of ​823,000 vehicles.

On ​Monday, Honda said it would build a $3 billion auto plant in Ohio that will be able to ​produce 240,000 hybrid ‌cars a year and start production in 2029.

articles.title: Big Tech has a spy problem
articles.summary: Silicon Valley is particularly vulnerable to corporate espionage: The cutting-edge technologies it develops have grown vital to the global economy.
articles.body: The PC revolution was upon us, and American tech companies were running circles around Compagnie des Machines Bull, the legendary but struggling French computer company. France was determined to find out how and why. Between 1987 and 1989, the Direction Générale de la Sécurité Extérieure, France’s equivalent of the CIA, planted moles inside the offices of Bull’s biggest American competitors, IBM and Texas Instruments, where the spies passed trade secrets back to the French company. The FBI and CIA ultimately uncovered the scheme and the employees were fired. Four decades later, the global Big Tech corporate espionage problem has grown – and so have the stakes. US-based Nvidia, the world’s largest and most important AI chipmaker, is investigating reports that it was a victim of a foreign surveillance effort. CEO Jensen Huang also acknowledged he had an extramarital affair. Although Huang and Nvidia haven’t provided details or connected those two revelations, The New York Times reported last week that the US State Department developed significant scrutiny of Huang’s relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed. Silicon Valley is particularly vulnerable to corporate espionage: The cutting-edge technologies it develops have grown vital to the global economy, and OpenAI, Google, Apple and many other high-profile tech companies in recent weeks and months have reported foreign and domestic spying attempts at their companies. “Corporate espionage has always been a big challenge, but today it’s especially so in areas where US firms are building technologies that are foundational to economic, military and other forms of power,” said Matthew Waxman, cybersecurity law professor at Columbia University. But Big Tech’s spy problem is almost certainly a lot bigger than anyone realizes. Man on the inside As IT exploded in economic import over the past several decades, information has become one of the world’s most valuable commodities. That has turned Big Tech’s secrets into the gold sitting in the underground vault – and made it rife for theft. AI has significantly intensified the battle for trade secrets. Cyberattacks and digital intrusions aren’t going anywhere. But the higher stakes of acquiring trade secrets have placed a renewed emphasis on human espionage inside corporations, said Greg Pollock, director of research and insights at risk management company UpGuard. “It’s true that huge amounts of data have been compromised through hacking, but the most important information is still what’s said in private,” Pollock said. The most sophisticated actors don’t choose only one path to gain access to trade secrets: Cyberattacks can help countries and companies steal information, but a human source can help advise what secrets matter and what decisions will be made about them, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government. Adversaries looking to obtain trade secrets through old-fashioned in-person espionage tend to accomplish that in one of two ways: hiring away employees who are willing to spill the beans or plant moles who befriend people. Having a human on the inside gives companies a potentially much longer timeframe to obtain information than via cyberattack alone – which tend to trip alarm bells after a while. Humans, by contrast, may be able to access key documents that could be related to their everyday tasks – or at least appear to be, noted Madhu Shashanka, cofounder of security firm Concentric AI. And, unlike computers, humans can gain the trust of employees, many of whom hold keys to crucial information. That makes anyone a target. “It’s not just the CEOs who are targeted, and it doesn’t all look like a James Bond movie,” said Krauthamer. “The average Silicon Valley employee knows to be on the lookout for phishing scams. But humans trust other humans. That’s just a growing risk.” Tip of the iceberg That risk long predates the computer era. Corporate espionage dates back to at least 1700, when French Jesuit priest François Xavier d’Entrecolles was sent on a mission to Jingdezhen, China – but not the kind of mission you’re probably thinking of. Imported Chinese porcelain was flooding the dining rooms of Europe’s elite in the early 18th century, and d’Entrecolles was sent to Jingdezhen, home of the country’s porcelain factories, to determine the manufacturing process that had stumped European porcelain makers. D’Entrecolles, who spoke Chinese, spent the next two decades touring factories and interviewing families to determine the secret behind Chinese porcelain. In 1712, he wrote his first letter to the treasurer of the Jesuits’ China missions with a details of the materials used, as well as the process for purifying, molding and firing the porcelain. Security experts agree that the corporate espionage problem has grown significantly over the past several hundred years – and particularly in the past decade. But how much it’s expanding can’t be fully known. US federal courts saw a record 1,500 trade secret cases filed last year. And high-profile cases have been a constant in the news lately. A month before the revelations of Huang’s affair, OpenAI said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” in one of its US offices planted by a Saudi employee who had used an internal productivity tool to determine when and where high-profile executives were meeting. (The former employee pleaded not guilty to the charges.) And in February, the US Justice Department indicted three former Google employees who were spying for foreign countries, including Iran. But the cases we know about are just scratching the surface of a potentially much more prevalent concern, said Elizabeth Rowe, a University of Virginia law professor specializing in trade secrets and intellectual property. “It’s a bigger problem than we are aware of,” said Rowe. “The ways these cases come to our attention tend to undercount how pervasive it is.” The most recent federal statute that criminalizes this espionage, passed in the late 1990s, relies heavily on companies self-reporting. Companies can also take civil action against adversaries, but that still relies on corporations speaking out. The problem: Businesses have many incentives not to talk about the problem of corporate espionage. Companies that go to court signal to investors that they lost potentially crucial information. Civil suits – particularly those dealing with complex trade-secret lawsuits – can be incredibly expensive. The biggest barrier: Filing a complaint exposes the trade secrets and makes them vulnerable to being lost through the lawsuit or the press. “All this suggests when you see a case that makes headlines, there are many, many more that never made it to the public,” said Rowe.

articles.title: Australian airline Qantas to axe 850 jobs at HQ, shift work to India
articles.summary: India is set to handle a major share of outsourced corporate operations of Australian airline Qantas, which plans to transfer around 850 head-office jobs
articles.body: India is set to handle a major share of outsourced corporate operations of Australian airline Qantas, which plans to transfer around 850 head-office jobs to technology services company Accenture under a multi-year agreement.Most of the services covered by the arrangement will be delivered by Accenture's teams in India, reported various Australian media outlets including Austrlia Broadcasting Company.The transition will cover several business functions, including finance, procurement, human resources and marketing. The first phase is expected to be implemented by mid-2027, with some services continuing to be handled in Australia.The arrangement is part of Qantas' efforts to overhaul its technology infrastructure and simplify its operations as artificial intelligence increasingly reshapes the travel industry. The airline is looking to modernise systems that have become difficult to integrate and manage.Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told employees that the company operates more than 1,000 legacy applications that were not designed to work together. “Modernising these systems and connecting the data across them is the critical next step,” she said, adding that the changes would help accelerate innovation and the airline's use of AI.Hudson also acknowledged the uncertainty the announcement could create among employees.“I know this is hard news for some, and I’m sorry for the uncertainty it brings,” she said.Explaining the broader objective, she added, “They are about modernising the technology behind our business and becoming more efficient, so we can keep investing in our customers, our people and our future.”The decision has drawn criticism from the Australian Services Union (ASU), which has questioned the implications of shifting work from Qantas' Australian headquarters to overseas teams.ASU NSW Secretary Angus McFarland said the union believed most of the affected positions were based at the airline's headquarters in Mascot, Sydney.“This should be chilling to not only those workers, but all Australians, because no Australian benefits from this. This is jobs offshore, and this is skills offshore at our national airline,” McFarland said, as quoted by ANI.The union has also alleged that the latest announcement contradicts assurances given to employees earlier this year.ASU Assistant National Secretary Scott Cowen said workers had been told in August that Qantas had no plans to offshore Australian jobs. “Earlier this year, Qantas told us directly there was no plan to offshore any jobs. Today, they’ve come out and told hundreds of staff members that their work will now be delivered mostly from people overseas,” Cowen said.The union is seeking details on how many positions will be affected, which roles will remain in Australia and what retraining assistance will be offered. It has also called for redundancy packages that take employees' years of service into account.What happens to affected Qantas employees?Hudson said the individual outcomes for employees had not yet been determined and that the airline would consult workers and their union over the coming months.Qantas has said it intends to retain as many employees as possible within the group by offering opportunities for redeployment, retraining and reskilling.The company is expected to work through these arrangements as the outsourcing transition progresses.You use AI every day. articles.title: Wall Street's $1.6 trillion rebound may look like a bottom — history says it often isn't: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Monday's rally came two sessions after the worst day in 18 months, and big bounces like it have usually been followed by one more trip below the low.
articles.body:
Dip buyers didn't wait long. Two sessions after the S&P 500's worst day in 18 months , stocks added more than $1.6 trillion in value, even as Nvidia kept sliding .

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was up about 2.3% Monday afternoon, its best day in seven months, while the Nasdaq-100 rose more than 3.4%, its best since May 2025.

Chip stocks did the heavy lifting. AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) jumped roughly 9% to 13%, adding more than $200 billion in combined market value — more than Nvidia's ( NVDA ) loss. Micron ( MU ), Applied Materials ( AMAT ) and Lam Research ( LRCX ) also climbed.

The hole is deep. The S&P 500 lost 4.4% on Nov. 5 — its worst day since the April 2025 tariff tantrum — and the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) closed Friday about 11% below its Oct. 6 record, putting it in correction territory.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has fallen 4% or more in a day and then gained 2% or more within three sessions 17 times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. That window captures Thursday's drop and Monday's bounce.

In 11 of those 17 cases, the index closed below the sell-off day close within three months. But a year later, it was higher 14 times, with a median gain of about 21%. Six of the 17 came during 2008-2009.

Last week's selling came from the top. "Hedge funds de-risked at a historic level," Nationwide chief market strategist Mark Hackett wrote Monday. By his count, their net bets on rising stocks sank to about the lowest in five years.

Everyday investors went the other way. "Institutions hit the panic button last week, while a surge in leveraged ETFs suggests retail investors were once again buying the fear," Hackett wrote.

The flows back him up. The Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF ( SOXL ), built to triple chip stocks' daily moves, took in a record $9 billion in October, according to Bloomberg data. It pulled in another $2.2 billion on Nov. 5 alone, the day chip stocks fell 12%.

"We had an aggressive sell on Thursday with, again, net buying from the ETF complex, net buying from payroll contributions," Dave Nadig said on Yahoo Finance's "Market Hang." "Lo and behold, Friday and Monday's payroll contributions show up, and we're back in the green."

Even one of Wall Street's best-known bears sees an end in sight. Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson said the correction is entering its "final phase."

The Nov. 5 close of 7,353.73 held about 30 points above the S&P 500's 200-day moving average . A close below it would fit the retest pattern. Holding above keeps the bounce intact into Tuesday's inflation report.

articles.title: Why Nvidia's alleged Chinese spy scandal is going to confuse markets — and the government
articles.summary: It's impossible to know where Beijing's intelligence scheme ends and Nvidia's genuine policy aims begin.
articles.body:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang is at the center of a massive scandal that's rocking the AI giant's stock.

It's also raising fresh questions about the company's relationship with China — and its stance on selling advanced technology to an economic adversary.

Huang admitted in a Nov. 8 memo to employees to an affair following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang (obviously no relation), whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. Nvidia's board has initiated an investigation.

Wall Street reaction so far has been negative but not catastrophic, with analysts questioning whether Huang will stay on while acknowledging how central he is to the company and the broader AI revolution . (Here's a suite of reactions .)

A key lesson in key-man risk if we've ever seen one.

But most critically, the Huang Affair has made it impossible to know where Beijing's alleged intelligence scheme ends and Nvidia's genuine policy aims begin. Everything is now in question.

In lobbying for looser export controls with China, was Huang motivated by revenue streams or an illicit romance? Getting entangled in a Chinese spy plot blurs the lines between the company's actual beliefs and what Chinese intelligence officials attempted to accomplish, sowing confusion in markets and the government.

"Regardless of the outcome of the investigation, however, we necessarily see Jensen losing some of his power/credibility in advocating for AI and Nvidia with US government representatives," Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson wrote.

It's hard to know and implausible to argue the difference between Nvidia's financial interests and China's intelligence scheme. Even if the alleged Chinese spy had zero influence on Huang's decision making and extracted zero intelligence from him and his company, Huang's messiness makes Nvidia appear impaired.

But Huang's importance atop the AI mountain makes him a crucial player in the US economy. President Trump and leaders in the tech world have come to his defense . The logic behind it is that Huang is so pivotal to American AI competitiveness that not even his irresponsible actions outweigh his worth and standing as a tech leader.

But Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a note on Monday that the investigation will boost major scrutiny of Nvidia and tip the thorny China chip export issue further toward bipartisanship.

"On the heels of last week's Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China," he said.

articles.title: Anthropic To Seek $1.4 Trillion Valuation in Blockbuster IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic’s debut on public markets will be unlike any that’s come before it, in ways that amount to either a once-in-a-generation opportunity — or a massive financial gamble, depending on whom you ask.
articles.body: Anthropic’s debut on public markets will be unlike any that’s come before it, in ways that amount to either a once-in-a-generation opportunity — or a massive financial gamble, depending on whom you ask. The startup behind the Claude AI assistant on Tuesday set a price range for its initial public offering of $70 to $78. If it prices at the midpoint, Anthropic will raise $61 billion in its IPO. That combined with options and unvested stock would value the company at roughly $1.1 trillion. At the top of the range, Anthropic could be worth $1.4 trillion. When Anthropic begins trading as soon as next week, there will be no analog to measure its performance against. The market has simply never seen a dedicated AI model developer go public. It is rare for a business to IPO as a public benefit corporation and, other than SpaceX, it is unheard of for any company to go public with a target valuation above $1 trillion. Anthropic’s IPO, expected to begin marketing to investors this week, is unconventional by almost any measure. The company promised in its pre-IPO regulatory filing that its technology would “bring forth an age of miracles” while simultaneously warning it may doom humanity. Still, the promise of a once-in-a-generation technological revolution (even with 90 pages of warnings and caveats in its more-than-300-page filing) could make Anthropic the biggest IPO in history. But there are other financial superlatives and quirks — not to mention persistent cold feet about AI on Wall Street — that will keep many investors on the sidelines. Bills keep coming due Despite rapid revenue growth, the five-year-old company has had only one quarter of operating profit, and it is on the hook for nearly $900 billion over the next few years — money it has committed to spend on computer power and data center infrastructure. Anthropic fans have held up its sales growth as a positive indicator of its financial health: The company brought in $17 billion in sales in the most recent quarter, up 1,127% from the same period a year earlier. And in the first nine months of this year, it recorded $33.2 billion in sales, versus just $4.6 billion in all of 2025. But by Anthropic’s own account, that kind of growth isn’t sustainable over the long term. “We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all,” the company said in its pre-IPO prospectus. At the same time, Anthropic relied on just five customers for a quarter of its sales this year. It didn’t disclose the five, but noted that some of them are also competitors. That points to a precarious situation in which a handful of companies have outsized control over Anthropic’s future cash flow. Any one of those companies, which may be building its own AI models to compete with Claude, may decide to scale back its own spending or walk away completely at any time. Ideally, investors would want to see a more robust customer base. Even bullish investors say that so-called concentration risk is worth keeping an eye on. Paul Marino, chief revenue officer at Themes ETFs, told CNN the relatively small number of major customers “gives me a little bit of concern” because their needs could change on a dime. “It’s something to monitor, but I’m not overly concerned with it because I’m one of those people that believes that AI is the future.” A chance to cash out Normally, when a company goes public, insiders can’t simply dump their shares on Day One and cash out — they have to hold on to them, usually for at least three to six months, to prevent the stock price from tanking. Anthropic’s lock-up schedule may be the most convoluted of any IPO in recent memory. The company opted for a complex, staggered schedule that permits some “non-founder” insiders to sell 10% of their holdings on Day One. The prospectus then lists some 23 dates over the first year when non-founder employees can dump more shares. Critics see that unorthodox schedule as another red flag, given the roughly $130 billion Wall Street insiders and venture capitalists have already poured into the company. “It has maxed out private investors, who now need the company to tap public markets to get them their payday,” financial research firm New Constructs wrote in a blog post. David Trainer, New Constructs’ founder and CEO, added in a call with CNN that he sees the payout to insiders as “a horrific misallocation of capital.” “We’re going to make a lot of people rich… that’s value that is taken away from public investors who are effectively giving them that from their own pockets, from their retirement accounts.” The concentration risk isn’t limited to Anthropic’s business customers. Critics also point to the concentration of power in the company’s special ownership structure, which gives its seven founders a majority of shareholder voting power. That novel approach has become more common in tech companies in recent years, but nonetheless raises concerns from some government officials. “We’re seeing a very worrisome trend of disempowerment to shareholders and all the balance of power tipping towards management,” New York City comptroller Mark Levine told Bloomberg News. Testing the AI trade Anthropic’s investor roadshow this week could hardly come at a worse moment for AI sentiment on Wall Street and beyond. Last week, AI-linked stocks tumbled on investors’ concerns that Democratic wins in Congress and state governments would slow the data center buildout. Americans’ sentiment about AI safety is in the gutter. And on Monday, Nvidia shares fell 5% after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair as his company announced it would be investigating him over foreign intelligence concerns. Anthropic, which declined to comment to CNN on its IPO plans, appears to be pressing ahead despite the turmoil. The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the company had meetings lined up with key investors this week and plans to list its shares Thursday or Friday next week, citing people familiar with the matter.

articles.title: JBS Profit Hit as China Quotas Overshadow US Beef Improvement
articles.summary: JBS NV is finally seeing some recovery in its US beef business, but the improvement wasn't enough to outweigh the impact of China's import restrictions on th...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- JBS NV ( JBS ) is finally seeing some recovery in its US beef business, but the improvement wasn't enough to outweigh the impact of China's import restrictions on the world's largest meatpacker.

Weaker results in the two crucial beef exporting regions of Brazil and Australia dragged third-quarter profits lower, as both countries hit an annual quota limit for shipments into China earlier this year. JBS's Brazil unit, which counts on the Asian country for a significant amount of its business, saw a 54% drop in adjusted earnings before items such as interest and taxes during the period.

The results underscore the challenges facing the global meat industry as a series of trade and supply disruptions hit giants like JBS. Beyond China's beef quotas and a US cattle shortage, new European Union rules have disrupted Brazilian beef shipments, the war in the Middle East has hurt key poultry markets, and a Newcastle disease outbreak in Brazil prompted some countries to restrict poultry imports.

While China's quota system is expected to remain in place through 2028, some pressure may ease ahead, according to Chief Executive Officer Gilberto Tomazoni. JBS already resumed production targeting shipments that are expected to arrive in China by January, when fresh annual quotas will be in place.

Overall, JBS reported adjusted earnings of 15 cents a share, a steep drop from 52 cents a year earlier.

That came despite some positive signs in the company's US beef business. The unit booked adjusted losses of $2 million before items including interest and taxes, narrower than the $42 million loss in the same period of 2025, according to IFRS accounting standards. On a US GAAP basis, the unit showed positive adjusted earnings.

"This year has started as a very challenging one, but we believe it will end much better," said Wesley Batista Filho, the head of US operations who is poised to take over as chief executive officer next year. "It's a year of inflection."

He said the resumption of cattle shipments from Mexico into the US is the main force aiding the market. Trade had been halted to prevent the spread of the deadly New World screwworm parasite, but imports resumed in late August, with more than 65,000 animals arriving at US ports through Oct. 30.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair appears to have short-circuited Wall Street analysts
articles.summary: Analysts take a wait and see approach on Jensen Huang.
articles.body:
If the Wall Street analysts who power consensus estimates are concerned about Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang's shocking affair with an alleged Chinese spy , they sure aren't showing it.

In its earnings preview on Nvidia ( NVDA ) released Monday at 5 a.m. ET, Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider didn't mention the issue once, even though it erupted over the weekend.

Citi analyst Atif Malik offered no opinion on the matter in a note out Tuesday, beyond outlining what investors are thinking.

"For investors, key issues are likely potential governance implications, increased regulatory scrutiny and export-control compliance of the flow of H200 chips into China (<1% of DC sales) and routed through other intermediaries, and longer-term impact on leadership stability. The company has stated that Mr. Huang will remain CEO while the investigation proceeds," Malik said.

Other top investment banks, such as JPMorgan, Evercore ISI and Jefferies, haven't published anything on Nvidia since the scandal broke. Nvidia lists 47 analysts covering the company.

"It's bizarre," one former sell-side analyst told me.

Having been a member of the consensus analyst community, I can tell you there could be several reasons for the initial silence.

One, a sharp critique of Huang could get an analyst cut off from management access. Considering how widely owned Nvidia's stock is and how important the company is to investment banks (acquisitions, stock buybacks, financings, etc.), being cut off isn't exactly great for job security.

Two, many of the analysts who cover Nvidia have known Huang for decades and have a relationship with him. They could be waiting to see how this shakes out.

Three, there could be little appetite to publish anything before the board's investigation concludes.

And lastly, some may remain fixated on Nvidia's pure fundamentals, which still look strong into 2027 even if Huang isn't CEO. Being the key player in the AI chip boom offers that luxury.

To be clear, analysts should be very concerned, as it's Huang who has powered the Nvidia discounted free cash flow model that has minted money for the clients of the biggest sell-side shops. Huang has made Wall Street stock analysts look like stock-picking heroes in the process!

But there is a real chance he won't be leading the company and driving its financial results for much longer, given the delicate predicament he has created for himself.

articles.title: Nvidia is worth nearly 30% less if Jensen Huang is no longer CEO: tech analyst
articles.summary: Nvidia's future hangs in the balance.
articles.body:
A big valuation haircut could be coming to what was once the world's most valuable company by market cap in Nvidia ( NVDA ) if newly embattled CEO Jensen Huang is forced to leave.

"We believe if Jensen was removed as CEO, Nvidia is worth a lot less (25%-30%) as a company/stock and would change the future direction of the company and create a dramatically different competitive environment around AI GPUs both in the US and globally especially for China," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives and veteran tech analyst Dan Ives said on Tuesday.

Nvidia's board of directors has launched an independent investigation into reports that a woman CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with was allegedly spying on him for the Chinese government.

Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees.

Nvidia stock fell 4.27% on Monday as a dark cloud settled over Nvidia and its once-Teflon CEO's future. Shares fell slightly in pre-market trading on Tuesday.

Added Ives, "Jensen is the core DNA of Nvidia and its AI success and ambitions are heavily tied to him staying on as CEO. Jensen is not replaceable..there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO and that speaks to the key man risk now with Nvidia that investors will factor this dynamic to the stock."

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: Dollar steadies as Waller argues for more rate hikes, inflation up next
articles.summary: By Javi West Larrañaga and Alun John GDANSK/LONDON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The dollar nudged higher on Tuesday following a bumpy few days, helped by hawkish rema...
articles.body:
GDANSK/LONDON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The dollar nudged higher on Tuesday following a bumpy few days, helped by hawkish remarks from Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller ‌ahead of US inflation data that could lift it further if rate hike bets strengthen.

Headline consumer ‌inflation is seen picking up to 3.9% and core inflation to 2.8% year-on-year in October, according to economists polled by Reuters, and ​a miss on either side would shape the direction for the dollar in the coming weeks.

"We've seen two consecutive stronger core CPI prints, so if we saw a third such print today, it would definitely add to concerns amongst market participants and also the Federal Reserve over the risk that higher energy prices are spilling over into broader ‌inflation pressure," said Lee Hardman, senior ⁠currency analyst at MUFG.

"That would obviously strengthen the need for the Fed to hike rates more, and the market would see that as a positive development for the dollar," ⁠he added.

A downside surprise "would reinforce the selling momentum that we've seen over the last 24 hours".

Waller, an influential Fed governor, got in ahead of the data, however, saying on Tuesday that the central bank ought to raise short-term borrowing costs ​next ​month even if inflation cooled last month. And he said ​it should consider an upsized half-point rate ‌hike if the inflation picture worsened.

Markets are now fully pricing a December rate hike from the Fed, upping expectations after those remarks.

That gave the dollar a small lift, but traders were still cautious ahead of the data.

The euro was 0.1% lower at $1.1215, while the pound lost 0.15% to $1.3423.

The dollar also gained around 0.2% on both the Japanese yen and Swiss franc, trading at 158.2 yen and 0.8209 francs, respectively.

That calm came after a dramatic ‌couple of sessions in currency markets.

A blowout October jobs report ​on Friday, with hiring more than twice the forecasts, sent the ​dollar surging, pushing the euro down 0.7%. That ​move then reversed on Monday, as a tumble in oil prices and gains for ‌stocks knocked the dollar lower.

The trade- and sentiment-sensitive ​Australian dollar rose by nearly ​1% through Monday to sit at $0.6918 on Tuesday and the New Zealand dollar gained even more, reaching $0.5634, with both fairly steady on Tuesday.

The kiwi caught an extra boost as results from last weekend's election ​suggested the incumbent three-party coalition would ‌stay in power, reducing uncertainty and the likelihood of any changes to the central bank's ​mandate.

(Reporting by Tom Westbrook in Sydney, Javi West Larranaga in Gdansk and Alun John in London ​Editing by Shri Navaratnam, DJ Yap and Joe Bavier)

articles.title: 3 bipartisan plans could slap new controls on semiconductor exports. Elizabeth Warren wants to pass one this year.
articles.summary: Three bipartisan measures circulating on Capitol Hill could reshape US export controls on semiconductors. On Monday, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren announc...
articles.body:
Three bipartisan measures circulating on Capitol Hill could reshape US export controls on semiconductors. On Monday, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren announced an effort to implement one in the coming weeks.

"It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA," Warren and Republican Jim Banks of Indiana said Monday as a rapidly growing scandal around Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang consumed Wall Street.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is a massive package that sets funding levels for the Department of Defense and is considered must-pass legislation in the coming weeks as lawmakers return to Washington after the elections.

The AI OVERWATCH Act could be attached to the NDAA and would require the Commerce Department to issue new, more restrictive licensing requirements for exporting certain advanced circuits.

The legislation has a bipartisan cast of 56 co-sponsors across the Senate and House versions of the bill .

A prominent Senate Democratic co-sponsor, in addition to Warren, is Charles Schumer of New York, who is expected to be Senate majority leader next year. In the House, likely incoming speaker Hakeem Jeffries also pushed for new chip restrictions in the must-pass bill on Monday, telling reporters there are provisions included in the Senate package that he supports.

"We're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version," Jeffries said.

There is, of course, plenty of legislative maneuvering to come — and President Trump has expressed his support for Huang. During a press conference late Monday afternoon, Trump called Huang an "amazing guy" while also revealing that the FBI is looking into the issue.

"I believe he is suffering greatly," Trump said of Huang.

But "the odds have increased that Congress will enact tougher export control legislation as part of the National Defense Authorization Act," Veda Partners wrote in a note to clients on Monday, adding that oversight of Nvidia "will also intensify this year and next Congress under Democrats' control."

The new push from Warren came after a New York Times report that the Commerce Department had an investigation into the Singaporean company suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China suddenly halted late last year after receiving an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information.

It was the latest twist in a rapidly evolving scandal that broke open Sunday when Nvidia's board launched an investigation into Huang's extramarital affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who was the CEO of Singaporean company Megaspeed International.

articles.title: Jensen Huang's spy scandal may cost Nvidia the China chip fight it was winning
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's spy scandal could revive Washington's push to ban China from US chips.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang was Washington's loudest voice against cutting China off from American chips, and his spy scandal is now the hawks' best argument. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department hasn't added a single company to its export ban list in 13 months.

The Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO admitted Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia stock fell about 4% Monday, even as chip stocks ( ^SOX ) jumped nearly 7%. That was Nvidia's worst day during a 5%-plus chip rally since Oct. 28, 1999, months after it went public.

The list in question is Commerce's Entity List . Companies on it need a US license to buy American technology, and those licenses are rarely granted. Commerce added 170 names in 2025 and 366 the year before. It hasn't added one since Oct. 9, 2025, by Yahoo Finance's count.

On Monday, Commerce extended its pause on a rule that would stretch those limits to companies majority-owned by listed firms. But only by two months, to Jan. 10, a week after a new Democratic Congress is sworn in.

"I think Commerce Department is going to batten down the hatches, and they're going to enforce export controls in a way that they weren't doing it before," Isaac Stone Fish, CEO and founder of Strategy Risks, told Deirdre Bosa on Monday .

The tech industry's own leaders see the stakes. "We lead in AI, and that means leading in power. It means leading in compute. It means leading in chips," Bret Taylor, OpenAI's chairman and CEO of AI startup Sierra, told Bosa on the same show . "AI is not particularly popular right now in this country," he added. "So I think this just introduces even more risk."

Huang's case against chip bans was simple. Cut China off, and it builds its own champion.

Huawei is his best exhibit. US sanctions knocked its sales from about $129 billion in 2020 to $95 billion two years later. Last year, it brought in about $123 billion, most of the way back, while building its own AI chips.

Stone Fish points instead to cars, where China absorbed Western know-how and then outbuilt its teachers. "Arguably the best car in the world is not American, Japanese or European, but it's Chinese, and export controls are a way of preventing that from happening," he said.

For Wall Street, it comes down to one person. "If he stays, then this is going to prove to be overdone, and this will be a strong buying opportunity. But if he doesn't stay, it's going to be a problem," Bernstein semiconductor analyst Stacy Rasgon told Bosa . "The only one that wins if he goes probably is China."
